data.title: Kennedy Center board votes to close main building for renovations
data.description:
The Kennedy Center board voted Tuesday to immediately close the venue’s main building for renovations, according to a source familiar, as the board argues that only President Trump can raise enough money to save it.

The vote comes after officials indicated that the performing arts center faces “certain fiscal collapse within weeks,” with a draft resolution describing the center as on the brink of bankruptcy, soon to be unable to make payroll or routine maintenance contracts. 

The board, handpicked by Trump, has also said the building was “unsafe for continued occupancy,” pointing to a recent water leak that caused a partial collapse of the grand foyer ceiling.

Minutes before the vote was scheduled to take place, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper again blocked the board’s attempt to add Trump’s name to the facade. It was the second time that the judge found the board’s action was likely unlawful. 

“Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” Cooper wrote. “The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted.”

The resolutions point to Trump’s fundraising skills as the center’s only saving grace. The board of trustees was restructured by the president last February, when he fired half the board and installed 14 new members.

“The Board understands that without such appropriate recognition it is unlikely that President Trump will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building and lead the fiscal rescue of the Center,” the resolution stated.

Justice Department attorneys, who are representing the Kennedy Center in the ongoing legal challenge, told Cooper during a hearing last month that the center was in “structural and financial disarray,” arguing further court intervention would impede the renovation project. 

Cooper rejected that notion as “not quite fair,” noting that his initial order in late May allowed “necessary maintenance and repair work” to continue.  

Trump’s name was added to the Kennedy Center earlier this year after a board vote in December 2025. But there was outrage over the addition of the Trump name, and Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member, brought a lawsuit to stop the name change.

The president’s name was stripped from the building in June after a ruling said it violated federal law, but in August, the board voted on a resolution that would re-add Trump’s name in the form of two inscriptions.

data.title: Crypto bill falls short in early hurdle on Senate floor
data.description:
A cryptocurrency regulation bill failed to advance on the Senate floor Tuesday, after all Democrats and a few Republicans blocked a procedural vote. 

The Senate voted 49-50 on a motion to proceed with consideration of the Clarity Act, failing to reach the required 60-vote threshold. It marks a major setback for the industry, which has long pushed for the measure setting up a regulatory framework for the crypto market. 

The vote Tuesday came amid a flurry of last-minute efforts to strike a deal between Republicans and crypto-friendly Democrats.  

About a dozen Democrats were considered potential yes votes. But they ultimately declined to support the legislation after the two sides failed to reach an agreement on ethics rules amid lingering concerns about President Trump and his family’s involvement in the crypto industry. 

Senate Republicans put forward what an aide described as their “last, best and final offer” on Sunday, unveiling updated bill text with changes to the ethics language and a several other sections at the heart of negotiations. 

The new White House-approved ethics provision builds on earlier language that barred public officials, including the president, from issuing or sponsoring crypto assets. 

It initially only gave enforcement power to the Department of Justice (DOJ). But after pushback from Democrats, the latest version also allows state attorneys general to bring cases against the agency or crypto exchanges over violations. 

This still fell short for Democrats. Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) suggested Monday that there were “a whole lot of loopholes” in the new ethics language. 

“I will tell you this: Democrats should not advance a bill that does not address the Trump family’s approach to this, where they’re clearly focused on enriching themselves,” he told reporters.

data.title: Talarico leads Paxton by 3 points in new Texas Senate poll
data.description:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico (D) is still leading his GOP challenger, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, according to a new poll released Tuesday.

The Telemundo/Mason-Dixon Polling & Research survey found the Democrat, a Texas state representative, held a three-point advantage over his Republican opponent less than two months out before November’s midterms.

Forty-six percent of the Texas voters surveyed supported the state lawmaker, while 43 percent backed the attorney general.

Additionally, three percent of respondents indicated they would vote for Libertarian Party candidate Ted Brown, and the remaining 8 percent said they were still undecided.

Talarico notably posted a strong lead among independent respondents, 51 percent of whom said they would support him over Paxton — who garnered just 30 percent of their backing. Thirteen percent of independents said they had yet to make up their mind about who they would vote for in this race. 

The state representative also had an 18-point advantage among Hispanic voters and 75-point edge with Black voters against his Republican opponent. Among white respondents, Paxton had an 18-point lead.

The Democrat has generally pulled ahead of Paxton after the Texas attorney general beat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the state’s GOP primary runoff in May. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, shifted its rating for this race from “leans Republican” to a “toss up” after Cornyn’s defeat.

Two June Siena University polls found the two candidates tied, first at 46 and then at 47 percent. By the end of July, Talarico had pulled ahead of Paxton by four percentage points in this polling center’s survey. 

Paxton had a narrow one-point advantage over the Democrat in an Emerson College poll conducted in early August, earning 47 percent of respondents’ support.

Almost a quarter of Texas voters Telemundo surveyed, 24 percent, said economic factors would most motivate how they cast their vote in the midterm races. Other major issues respondents identified were inflation and living costs — amounting for 23 percent of responses — as well as immigration at 18 percent.

Economic concerns have been top of mind for voters across the nation this election cycle, amid surging energy prices during the ongoing Iran war and President Trump’s tariff fight with Canada. 

The Telemundo poll was conducted among a total of 625 registered Texas voters from Sept. 8-10 with an approximately 4 percentage point error margin.

data.title: Dem rep asks Bessent to 'talk sense' into Trump on regulating AI
data.description:
Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch (Mass.) on Tuesday urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to convince President Trump to reverse course on regulating artificial intelligence (AI).

During Bessent’s appearance before the House Financial Services Committee, Lynch said Trump does not have “a grasp” of “what we’re dealing with” regarding AI.

“I’ll be honest, I don’t think the president could spell AI if I gave him the first letter,” quipped the Massachusetts Democrat, the ranking member of a House Financial Services subcommittee focused on AI.

The Commerce Department has worked with leading AI labs on evaluating models before they are deployed, under a voluntary program.

Earlier this summer, the Trump administration briefly held up new models from OpenAI and Anthropic, before allowing the companies to release their GPT 5.6 and Fables and Mythos models, respectively.

Trump has dismissed the need for beefed-up regulations on AI, even as industry leaders argue for reigning in the pace of development. Trump said Monday the only “guardrails” AI needs is a “STRONG AND SMART” president.

The president wrote on Truth Social, “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!” adding there is a “SICK conspiracy” in the U.S. against AI and data centers.

During Tuesday’s hearing, Lynch credited Bessent with “suggesting some things” on AI “that are thoughtful and … cautionary.” The veteran lawmaker later said “we’ve lost control” of AI, referencing OpenAI recently hacking the systems of Hugging Face, which Nvidia announced it will purchase earlier this month.

“Do you think the president understands that it probably doesn’t matter whether the good guys develop a superintelligence or the bad guys develop a superintelligence?” Lynch remarked. “If you don’t have control of that entity, and it has preferences and goals that are inimical to the existence humanity, it won’t matter.”

Bessent pushed back, saying it “matters a great deal” whether the U.S. or China lead on AI. Lynch then cut the Treasury secretary off, reiterating his view that “the entity itself is what is the danger to us all,” not the possibility of China leading on AI.

“We keep hearing about this race, this race against China. … Well, we don’t control the entity that we’re trying to create, and neither does China,” Lynch said.

“What I’m saying is, I hope there’s a way that you might be able to talk sense to the president about AI and the threat that you and I know it presents,” the Massachusetts lawmaker later told Bessent.

Bessent responded saying Trump was “completely aligned” with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on AI development. While Huang was speaking at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles on Monday, Trump called him and said concerns about AI were a “hoax.”

“The data centers are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy,” the president said after Huang put him on speaker phone, according to a video summit attendee Ben Pouladian shared online.

Earlier this month, Huang urged policymakers to regulate “practical and actual” harms of AI instead of “theoretical and hypothetical” effects.

“We want to make sure that the technology advances in a safe way and … the more advanced it is, the safer and more practical it could be,” Huang told reporters at the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, N.C.

data.title: Watch live: House unveils McCarthy's official Speaker portrait
data.description:
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is hosting a ceremony at the Capitol Tuesday afternoon to unveil the official portrait of his predecessor, former Rep. Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.).

Rep. Patrick McHenry (R-N.C.) briefly took over as Speaker pro tempore following McCarthy’s historic ouster in 2023. The California Republican irked his GOP colleagues after making concessions to Democrats during a long government spending battle, amid other criticisms.

Johnson was later voted in to replace McCarthy and the former Speaker resigned from office in December 2023.

Former GOP Reps. John Boehner (Ohio) and Newt Gingrich (Ga.), who also held the gavel, and Marjorie Taylor Greene (Ga.) — who strongly supported McCarthy — are among the expected guests for the ceremony.

The event is scheduled to begin at 3 p.m. EDT.

Watch the live video above.

data.title: Republicans may gain nothing from redistricting: DDHQ
data.description:
Republicans aiming to gain seats in Congress after several GOP-controlled states redrew their congressional maps in the last year may gain nothing in the November midterm elections, according to the election handicapper Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

DDHQ’s election forecast on Tuesday shows Democrats having a 68 percent probability of winning the House compared to Republicans’ 32 percent.

“In Decision Desk HQ’s forecast, Democrats not only achieve an average gain of 13 seats in the states with unchanged boundaries, they also gain an average of two seats across the nine states that redistricted,” DDHQ chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley wrote on Substack.

Democrats won an average seat majority of 229-206 across the forecast’s 1 million simulations, resulting in a 14-seat gain, Skelley wrote. But factoring in the states with redrawn congressional maps, he said that Democrats make an average gain of 13 seats in the 41 states that did not redistrict, which Skelley emphasized as being the party’s “path to a majority.”

“In our forecast for the unchanged states, Democrats win an average of nearly 150 seats, up from the 137 they currently control,” he continued. “Meanwhile, the redistricted states do not come close to offsetting that shift.”

He explained how in Texas, “Republicans are averaging a bit under a two-seat gain, roughly three seats short of their ideal.” Texas was the first state to redraw its map after President Trump urged red states to redistrict in order to maintain and increase their majority in Congress, with other red states following suit.

Redrawn districts that are home to Latino majorities give Texas Democratic incumbents a slight advantage, with Reps. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) and Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) both forecasted to keep their seats.

“Similarly, they also have around a 1 in 3 chance of defeating two-term GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in the 15th District,” Skelley continued. “While Trump would have won that seat by roughly 18 points under the new lines, he only would have won it by about two points in 2020.”

Florida could also see Republicans underperform more, with no shift favoring Republicans despite redistricting targeting four Democratic-held seats, with at least two of those seats both being favorites to hold on, Skelley wrote.

Ohio holds a similar likelihood of underperforming, with three Democrats likely to keep their seats and Rep. Max Miller’s (R-Ohio) district shifting toward a toss-up amid allegations of domestic abuse in connection with his wife.

The first Democratic-led state to retaliate with its own ballot measure to redraw its map could give California four seats out of the five where it could see gains. But Skelley said that Rep. David Valadao (R-Calif.) is the “smaller underdog” on “turf that Trump narrowly would have won in 2024” in the 22nd District.

“A potential Republican win there, as well as outside shots in districts such as the 13th, 45th, and GOP-held 48th [districts] help keep Democrats from averaging the full-on five-seat gain they want in California,” Skelley added.

Missouri has been the latest front in the redistricting battle. The state’s Supreme Court earlier this month unanimously ruled that the redrawn map designed to benefit Republicans “did not go into effect and will not go into effect” unless voters approve it in a referendum in the fall.

Skelley said DDHQ has a freeze on Missouri’s forecast until the legal battle over the map “is finalized.”

The high court said that the state must use the old map that favored the GOP six seats to two rather than replace it with the 7-1 House map used during this year’s primaries. The decision has confused Missouri voters as to which primary candidates will appear on the ballot. It has also made them angry, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-Mo.) previously told The Hill.

Trump called the ruling a “Dark Day for ‘Justice’ in Missouri” and claimed that the election process had been, “as usual … disturbed.”

data.title: 'This is a jobs bill': Jon Voight, film industry leaders make push for federal tax credit
data.description:
Jon Voight is joining a bipartisan group of lawmakers touting the need for a federal film and TV production tax credit, saying a new report shows such an incentive would “level the playing field and bring jobs back to our country.”

The “Deliverance” star, whom President Trump named last year as one of his “special ambassadors” to Hollywood, was on hand on Tuesday as the Motion Picture Association (MPA) released a study by Olsberg SPI that it commissioned to measure the potential economic impact of a federal tax incentive.

According to the report, such a credit would add an average of more than 143,000 jobs annually across the country and boost production expenditures in the U.S. by more than $125 billion from 2027 to 2035.

Voight said American film producers — often enticed by generous incentives offered by other countries — have told him that they “would like to work in the United States, but it’s not economically possible.”

“I received a call from one of the producers of one of our big blockbuster series of films, and he said to me, ‘Jon, we can’t make films in Hollywood. We can’t make films in the United States,'” he said.

“Now thousands upon thousands of our people are out of the work they love and are struggling to find ways to put to put food on the table for their families. It’s a very serious situation, and it breaks my heart,” Voight said.

While acknowledging “Congress is not my bailiwick,” the 87-year-old Academy Award winner said lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have shown “strong energy” to back legislation in support of a federal tax incentive.

“This legislation will create a massive number of jobs in the entertainment industry throughout the entire United States,” Voight said. 

In a Truth Social post earlier this month that drew rare bipartisan support, Trump pushed for a federal tax incentive for movie and TV productions, urging Democrats and Republicans in Congress to work together to “immediately craft legislation to save the movie, television, and entertainment business in America.”

“The federal incentive will be a game changer for our industry,” Charles Rivkin, MPA’s chairman and CEO, said on Tuesday. 

Reps. Laura Friedman (D-Calif.) and Brian Jack (R-Ga.) emphasized the bipartisan “tremendous momentum” behind the issue, stressing that it’s not “about movie stars” or Hollywood handouts. 

“We’re not talking about abstract, large companies. We’re talking about our neighbors,” Friedman said.

“We’re talking about the people who live and are supported by the economy in so many of our cities and states. These are costumers, set designers, drivers, carpenters, caterers, dry cleaners, cafe owners,” she said. 

“They are people just looking to do something that they think is aspirational and that will provide a good union job for themselves, and that they could raise their family on,” Friedman noted, saying she and Jack are currently working on drafting legislation.

“Most of the Marvel films filmed from the mid-2010s up until a few years ago, were made in my district,” Jack said. 

“Unfortunately, in recent years, many of those movies have left for overseas,” the House freshman said. 

“The real-world impact is that I represent craftsmen, technicians, electricians that now are on second, third, fourth jobs because the jobs they thought they were moving to Georgia for are no longer there,” Jack said. 

“Global investment and global spending on the entertainment industry is at an all-time high — just not here. It’s diminishing here,” said SAG-AFTRA president Sean Astin, citing the MPA-commissioned report.

“The value of this art form, of this craft, of this storytelling, is being recognized by governments all over the world,” Astin said.

“They recognize that it’s a good investment to put their money where their mouth is and bring the jobs and the business to their areas,” he said. 

“At the end of the day, this is a jobs bill,” Rivkin said at the virtual briefing, also attended by International Brotherhood of Teamsters President Sean O’Brien, producer Steven Paul, former Directors Guild of America president Thomas Schlamme, International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees president Matthew Loeb and other members of the U.S. Film and Television Production Coalition.

“When any major motion picture films in the United States, it injects about $1.3 million a day into the local economy, and the people that that impacts are not necessarily just the stars on the screen,” Rivkin said, adding he had never experienced such “broad and powerful bipartisan” support on any effort.

Friedman stressed that getting the federal tax incentive done is a “top priority” for lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

“In terms of the timing, the best time to have done this would have been maybe four years ago, five years ago,” Friedman said.

“The second best time would be tomorrow.”

data.title: Live updates: Blanche to brief press in White House Rose Garden; Kennedy Center loses bid to add Trump's name
data.description:
Attorney General Todd Blanche is set to brief reporters in the Rose Garden on Tuesday, becoming the latest administration official to step in since the departure of former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt. It’s an unusual venue for a briefing.

A judge once again ruled the Kennedy Center could not inscribe President Trump’s name on the exterior of the performing arts center, saying it needs congressional approval.

FBI Director Kash Patel testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee for an oversight hearing on Tuesday morning.

Ahead of the meeting, Patel released a letter sent to panel chair Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) to explain expenditures that have drawn scrutiny. But questioning during the hearing turned to an unexpected topic: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) grilled Patel as he tried “to understand” a recent change in policy regarding bestiality. The line of questioning was sparked by a shift in FBI hiring practices that lifted longtime bans on selecting new trainees if they have engaged in prostitution or bestiality.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spent the morning in the House Financial Services hearing, facing questions on tariffs, artificial intelligence and more.

Earlier Tuesday, Trump upbraided the Supreme Court for its 7-2 ruling against his mail-in ballot restrictions the evening prior.

“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won’t be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Follow along live below.

data.title: Prosecutors drop death penalty for Nick Reiner for alleged murders of parents
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Prosecutors are no longer seeking the death penalty against Nick Reiner, who is accused in the double murders of his parents, director Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner. 

Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman announced his decision Tuesday, saying the maximum sentence Reiner can now receive is life in prison without the possibility of parole if convicted.

Hochman said he had discussed taking the death penalty off the table with Reiner’s siblings before making the decision.

The son had previously been charged with first-degree murder, but prosecutors secured a special circumstance enhancement that alleges he was lying in wait to murder them. The special circumstance can increase potential penalties in the sentencing phase of a trial to life in prison without parole.

He was indicted by a grand jury last month. The indictment will expedite the case to a jury, bypassing a preliminary hearing. 

Reiner had previously pleaded not guilty to the killings of his parents. 

Rob and Michele Singer Reiner honored at the Emmys

Rob Reiner was honored during the Emmy Awards on Monday night.

Actress Jamie Lee Curtis gave a tribute to Rob Reiner, who won a posthumous award for outstanding guest actor in a comedy series for his appearance in FX’s “The Bear.”

“He was generous and kind and funny as hell and a friend to all,” Curtis said. 

The couple was found stabbed to death in their Southern California home after their daughter discovered them in late 2025. Reiner was later arrested and jailed without bail in connection with the murders.

Documents from the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health stated the couple died within “minutes” of receiving “multiple sharp force injuries” with a “knife, by another.”

Reiner, who lived with his parents, had previously spoken openly about his struggles with drug addiction and periods of homelessness and co-wrote a movie inspired by his struggles with his father.

data.title: Watch live: Blanche briefs reporters from Rose Garden
data.description:
Attorney General Todd Blanche will speak with reporters Tuesday afternoon in the White House Rose Garden.

Few details are known about the briefing, but it marks only the second since former press secretary Karoline Leavitt resigned from the post. The DOJ has played a major role in arguing on behalf of President Trump’s immigration and anti-fraud moves, as well as the White House ballroom and Kennedy Center renovations.

The event also comes as the president faces scrutiny over his response to AI leaders’ warning about the risks of the rapidly evolving technology and his vow to give adults in the U.S. a $5,000 dividend if the GOP maintains control of both chambers of Congress next year.

The briefing is scheduled to begin at 2 p.m. EDT.

Watch live above.
